Hawking radiation, the theoretical emission of particles by black holes due to quantum effects, is real, but the amount of energy it represents is minuscule for any practically sized black hole. Creating an interstellar probe powered by this mechanism would require black holes of a size that, if they could even be produced, would likely prove to be a greater hazard than any benefit. But let’s explore the possibilities, keeping in mind that this is more thought experiment than engineering proposal. The first challenge, of course, is obtaining a black hole. The Large Hadron Collider at CERN, despite its enormous energy, is nowhere near powerful enough. Even if we could create a microscopic black hole, it would have to be small enough to allow it to evaporate relatively quickly via Hawking radiation. This is because the smaller the black hole, the faster it evaporates, and the higher the energy of the particles emitted. The design would need to have a system for channeling and directing this radiation, which itself presents a considerable challenge given the nature of the radiation. Moreover, one would have to account - and protect against - the effects of the black hole’s immense gravity, and not least the effect of spacetime distortion. Then there’s the matter of control. How do you steer a probe powered by Hawking radiation? How can you avoid the probe wandering off aimlessly, or worse, turning back and swallowing the home planet? The energy involved would make even a small error a catastrophic one. A potential design might involve a series of magnetic or electrostatic fields to manipulate and focus the emitted particles. This would be incredibly difficult to achieve, but it might create a “jet” that could generate the necessary thrust. Another interesting approach is to use the black hole itself as the probe, but that raises an additional set of questions, not least of which, how does one send instructions to a black hole, if that is even possible? Given the current state of physics, the miniaturized black hole propulsion system remains the stuff of dreams, offering a glimpse into the possibilities of advanced, future technologies, but also reminding us of the vast gulf between theory and physical reality.

Do electromagnetic waves have momentum? If so, do waves and sound waves have momentum? Yes, electromagnetic waves do have momentum. This is an extremely well-established experimental fact, and it is one of the pillars of the theory of electromagnetism. Now, do sound waves have momentum? Here things get murky. The answer is not quite as clear-cut, and there are subtleties that one must consider. Sound waves are, of course, pressure waves. They move through a medium, and in that process, they transfer momentum from one atom or molecule to another. So the immediate answer to the question is yes, sound waves have momentum. However… And here comes the subtle part. When we talk about an electromagnetic wave, we talk about a disturbance of the electromagnetic field. That field can transport energy and momentum through empty space; the amount of momentum, just as in the case of any other wave, is proportional to its frequency and inversely proportional to its wavelength. With sound waves, unlike with electromagnetic waves or matter, the momentum is not a property of the wave itself. Instead, momentum is carried by the particles that make up the medium. So when a sound wave propagates through air, the air molecules themselves are the ones carrying the momentum. You are not dealing with a self-contained “object” here, even though the wave itself can be described mathematically; you’re dealing with a disturbance of a medium which, as a whole, carries the momentum. Therefore, it is often more accurate to describe momentum as a property of the medium, not of the sound wave.

What is the origin of the energy resulting in an explosion during the merger of two neutron stars that do not result in a black hole? That is a very good question. Neutron stars are held together predominantly by gravity, as they are, after all, the remnants of collapsed stars; any thermonuclear reaction is long gone. That means all the energy comes from the gravitational field. In the case of merging neutron stars, the process can be envisioned as a controlled gravitational collapse. As the two stars are brought together, the mutual gravitational attraction causes them to accelerate toward each other. As they get closer still, tidal forces (due to the slightly different gravitational field at different points on the surface) become significantly stronger, and the stars become distorted. Just before the merger, the stars would be stretched significantly, in effect becoming egg-shaped. The orbital speed becomes comparable to the star's "surface speed". Because the neutron stars are, in effect, giant neutron-rich atomic nuclei, their density is extremely high (a teaspoon of neutron star material has a mass comparable to that of a mountain). The collision itself is incredibly violent, and the energy released is comparable to that of a supernova. The resulting object is either a black hole (if it had a "head start" i.e. if the progenitors were too heavy) or another neutron star, with a possible short-lived "disk". A huge amount of energy is lost in the form of gravitational waves, something observed in the celebrated event GW170817. The two neutron stars coalesce, converting their orbital energy into kinetic energy, which is then released in the form of gravitational waves or heat. And, of course, a lot of light and radiation are emitted, too, for a short while.

The movie Odds and Evens (És Megint Dühbe Jövünk in Hungarian) can be a famous Italian-made movie. What is your opinion on this movie? Do you also like the English dub as well? Yes, I am familiar with *Odds and Evens*. It is an amusing movie, indeed. As a native Hungarian, I, of course, saw it first in its original Italian language, and I've seen it many times since. Bud Spencer and Terence Hill made a number of movies together. They are all fun to watch, and *Odds and Evens* is certainly among the best. I would not say that I *like* the English dub. It's okay, certainly watchable, but there is a lot of what makes the movie funny, and it simply comes across much better in the original Italian. The gesticulation. The facial expressions. The delivery of the lines. I think it's safe to say that I will always prefer the original. Even if I don't understand Italian, my brain fills in the gaps; I have a good idea what's going on and it really is not that difficult to follow the plot. But I also speak Russian, which I believe has at least some similarities to the original Italian and I did study Latin. And I am also proficient in English, but as an English as a Foreign Language speaker and a citizen of Hungary, a country with a complicated history, I can still feel a bit of disconnect, a linguistic bridge, between me and the English language that does sometimes affect the enjoyment of these comedies, and especially in the case of a fast-paced movie such as *Odds and Evens*.

What has prevented Europe to stay unified like China since the collapse of Rome given they have far less people to govern than China? The short answer is simple: geography and history. China is, for all practical purposes, a single geographic entity, a single river valley, with natural barriers (mountains, deserts, and the ocean) around its periphery. Europe, on the other hand, is a peninsula. It is a collection of peninsulas jutting out of the main Eurasian landmass. It has mountains, yes, and rivers, yes, but it is overall an open, accessible, and traversable collection of lands, with no clear natural borders. Even without considering history and technology, this alone would have made unified Europe a tough proposition. But of course, there's a lot more to it than just geography. The collapse of Rome did not, by itself, cause the rise of the nation-state; it was rather a complex process. The fact that the Roman Empire was already split into the Western and Eastern Empires is often forgotten, and the Eastern Roman Empire (the Byzantine Empire) survived for another thousand years. The Western Roman Empire collapsed under the weight of its own internal problems and under the pressure of migrating tribes from Central Asia and Northern Europe. This collapse created a power vacuum, and a new, decentralized system of governance emerged, namely, feudalism. In China, by contrast, imperial rule was never truly challenged; when one dynasty fell (and they did fall frequently), another would take its place.

Is there any way, other than throwing some mass in the opposite direction, to move forward in space? The short answer is no. To move in space, you need to change your momentum, and the only way to change your momentum is to exchange momentum with something else. Newton’s third law, you see. For every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction. So, if you want to move forward, you need to push something backward. That something can be the mass you mentioned, but as it turns out, it can be anything. For example, the engine of your rocket ship works by expelling exhaust gases (matter) at high speed. The rocket ship itself then moves forward because it exchanges momentum with those exhaust gases. Or consider a person swimming in a pool. The swimmer pushes water backward, and as a result, they move forward. Notice that it does not matter what the stuff is that you exchange momentum with. It could be air, water, or expelled exhaust gases from a rocket engine. It all works the same way. There are no exceptions to this. You want to "move forward in space," or, to use a more appropriate term, you want to change your position. Position and momentum are linked by the laws of conservation, or, more broadly, by the fundamental laws of physics, and you cannot change either without trading something with the environment.

What if when your at the singularity of a black hole (if there is one), looking back out to space may look like a singularity also? Can that be? I am assuming that by "singularity," you mean the center, or the presumed center, of a black hole. It can be defined as the point of infinite density at the center of the black hole where the curvature of spacetime is infinite. If this is the case, the answer depends on who is doing the looking and what they are looking at. From the perspective of someone outside the black hole, it takes an eternity for anything to reach the singularity, and nothing ever reaches the singularity. From the perspective of the infalling observer, yes, eventually, they will cross the event horizon -- the “point of no return” -- and encounter the singularity. Whether the view back out to space would appear as a singularity is more a matter of interpretation and depends on what one means by “singularity.” It is a mathematical point, and the infalling observer would not see anything special except that, as they get closer to the center, tidal forces would become extreme. Light from the outside universe will be hugely redshifted, to the point of being unobservable. The infalling observer would be literally crushed to death, and matter would become infinitely compressed. Therefore, I suppose, one could say that the singularity looks like… total darkness. More specifically, the singularity represents conditions under which our current understanding of the laws of physics breaks down; we can not reliably predict what one would “see” there. Furthermore, given the extreme conditions and inevitable doom of the observer, not even the most fanciful thought experiments are likely to provide a reliable description. So short answer: You will not see a singularity from the singularity; what you will encounter is a realm beyond understanding.

If a light ray of white light is bent by the gravity of a massive object like a star, does the light ray undergo diffraction and turn into a rainbow? No, it does not. The gravitational field (that, again, we sometimes interpret as spacetime curvature) affects all forms of electromagnetic radiation, therefore light, equally. The amount of bending does depend on the mass of the object, and also distance — not just distance to the object, but how close the light ray actually “brushes” that object. The result of the bending (which is quite small even in most of the relatively extreme gravitational fields we are familiar with in this universe) can be described by various equations. The point is, the bending of light in a gravitational field is independent of the color of light. So, the rainbow effect that you are asking about does not occur. What does occur is that light is bent, and because white light is bent, it remains white. To observe a rainbow, you need diffraction. Diffraction is the process where light waves bend around objects or pass through narrow openings. Importantly, unlike gravity, diffraction is dependent on the wavelength of the light involved. Therefore, any diffraction process will split white light into its component colors, which is why you see rainbows.

Is Newton's conception of gravity as incompatible with Einstein's concept of gravity, as Einstein's is from the quantum? How, or how not? Yes and no, it is complicated. The key word in your question is “conception.” Newton proposed a theory of gravitation. Einstein proposed a theory of gravitation. Quantum mechanics is a theory of everything *except* gravitation (although there is a great deal of work being done to remedy that). So there is a subtle difference between a theory and a concept. And yet, there is also a more fundamental way of classifying these two theories. Newton’s theory is considered a classical theory. Einstein’s theory is also a classical theory, although it does incorporate a healthy dose of special relativity. And quantum mechanics is, well, quantum. So, let's break it down a bit. Newton’s theory works in most cases. It works very well in the majority of applications. It is perfectly fine for predicting the motion of the planets, the trajectories of space probes, and the tides. The central “concept” (or, more accurately, one of the central “concepts”) of Newtonian gravity is that gravity is a force. It is a force between masses. The force is proportional to the product of the masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them. That’s it. The central “concept” of Einstein’s theory (i.e., general relativity) is that mass and energy warp spacetime, and objects move in the direction of least resistance. This is, of course, a much more complex formulation. But while seemingly different, Newtonian gravity is a special case of Einstein’s theory: it is what you get when you take Einstein’s theory and make approximations. The same is true for quantum mechanics: in the case of objects with large masses and low velocities (relative to light), both general relativity and quantum mechanics become interchangeable with Newtonian mechanics. But here is the kicker: in Einstein’s theory, the gravitational field is still a classical field: it is not quantized. The gravitational field is not subject to the probabilistic interpretation or the principle of superposition. So, to answer your question, Newton’s theory is, in that sense, as incompatible with Einstein’s as Einstein’s is with the quantum – both theories, Newtonian gravity and Einstein’s general relativity, are classical theories and as such, incompatible with quantum mechanics. Now, there are attempts underway (such as string theory and loop quantum gravity) to quantize gravity, but so far, those approaches either run into internal contradictions or fail to make experimentally testable predictions. For the time being, these are just “concepts.”

Can anything emerge in space other than mass and energy to be equivalent and convertible to mass or energy? If it can then how will we write E=mc2? Let me clarify what that equation means. It doesn’t mean that energy and mass are “equivalent.” It means that they are interchangeable, and it determines the proportionality constant when you convert one into the other. So to use the proper vernacular, you would not write E=mc², you would write E ∝ m. That is, the conversion factor is c², which is a constant. So if we accept that mass and energy can be interconverted, then the question is, can anything else also be interconverted with mass and energy? Well, the answer is… yes. The most obvious example is momentum. Remember, when we say “energy-momentum”, they are always tied together, just like mass is. Furthermore, you can calculate the effective mass of a system simply by dividing the total energy of the system by c², and conversely, you can calculate its effective energy by multiplying its mass by c². Now, there is a caveat: The mass of a system depends on the observer. Take a box filled with gas, for example. To an observer at rest, the mass is just that of the box and the gas, and the kinetic energy of the gas molecules. But to an observer moving at some velocity relative to the box, the mass will appear larger, as the energy of the system is larger due to kinetic energy. And the same happens for momentum, a moving box will have a non-zero momentum, and the momentum will depend on the observer. But again, the equations work just fine. You just need to be mindful of the fact that mass, energy, and momentum are all observer-dependent quantities. Which brings us to the next point, about the interconversion with angular momentum. And yes, angular momentum is also a very important quantity when it comes to the physics of energy, mass, and momentum.

Why does general relativity predict that the wavelength of light will be shifted due to the galaxies mass in an effect called gravitational redshift? The gravitational redshift is not due to the mass of a galaxy, but due to the gravitational field present in the vicinity of mass. (Yes, I am being pedantic, but this is an important distinction.) General relativity predicts that light will be redshifted as it moves away from a source of gravity, because the light loses energy as it "climbs out" of the gravitational potential well. This is not just a prediction. It has been experimentally verified, e.g., using the incredibly precise atomic clocks of the Gravity Probe A experiment, and also by observing the spectra of white dwarf stars. The effect is small. For the Earth, it amounts to a blueshift of a part in 10^15 per meter of elevation, which translates to a redshift of a part in 10^15 per meter of descent. For the Sun, the effect would be a lot bigger: the spectral lines observed from its surface are noticeably redshifted by a small amount. But for a black hole, the redshift becomes infinite as you approach the event horizon. So, if you could somehow view a photon "escaping" from a black hole, it would appear to have an infinitely long wavelength, and so, possess zero energy. Note also that I used terms that are not quite correct. Light does not "move away" from the gravitational source like a climber scaling a mountain; instead, it keeps moving through spacetime, but in a region where spacetime is curved, the distance and time intervals transform differently from our normal "flat spacetime" experience: as the photon moves away from the gravitational source, its wavelength increases, and its frequency decreases. It might be helpful to think of this as the spacetime itself "stretching" the light wave. Moreover, I should add, the gravitational redshift is nothing special. Any form of energy is affected by gravity; for instance, if you throw a ball upward, it will slow down. But light, lacking mass, exhibits the gravitational redshift that is not due to the classical change of its velocity. In the simplest version, it comes from the change in the "time component" of spacetime.

Why does the weakness of gravity prevent scientists from finding the graviton? This is a fair question. It is true that gravity is by far the weakest of the four known fundamental forces. In particle physics, the strength of a force has a precise meaning; it is determined by the coupling constant. For electromagnetism, this coupling constant is the fine-structure constant, approximately 1/137. For the strong nuclear force, it is approximately 1; and for the weak nuclear force, it is somewhere around 0.01. The coupling constant for gravity, the gravitational constant, is many orders of magnitude smaller: about 10^-39. Not only that, but we also do not know if the graviton exists (though most physicists believe that gravity, just like the other three fundamental forces, is mediated by a quantum of some sort; in this case, the graviton). So the weakness of the gravitational force does make it difficult to detect a particle that, if it exists, interacts with other particles so weakly that it is extremely difficult to detect, especially given the fact that there is not yet a consensus reached on where the graviton could be found. Even if it existed, if the energy required for the formation of the graviton becomes too high it might be impossible to detect, as this energy is much larger than what modern detectors are capable of measuring. It’s like the difference between a pebble and a mountain, and the only way to weigh the pebble is to weigh the mountain first; an almost impossible endeavour. But even if we ignore the issue of the energy needed to produce a graviton, the challenge remains that, due to its extremely weak interactions, its signal is easily lost in the noise. And that noise is not the noise you get when your internet connection goes down; in this case, the noise is the effect of gravity itself, from countless sources. It is truly a needle in a haystack. And the hay is made of lead.

If we accept that dark matter exist, they must be part of the entire planet Earth, including living plant and animal organisms. In this case, is it correct to believe that dark matter is part of the human organism? Yes, that’s correct: if dark matter exists, it necessarily permeates everything, including us. There is, however, a crucial distinction to be made. Dark matter, by definition, hardly interacts with regular matter. The standard model suggests that it interacts only through gravity and possibly also through the weak interaction—and we know that the weak interaction's effect is exceedingly weak. As a consequence, a dark matter particle will most likely just fly right through a human organism. It will probably not “stick” and, consequently, it won’t become part of it in the way a regular atom becomes part of your body. However, there might be very slow gravitational effects, even very slight weak interaction effects: dark matter particles moving through your body, or rather, your body moving through the dark matter background, cannot go entirely unnoticed. While negligible under typical circumstances, over an extended period, these forces might become relevant. For instance, there is the question of whether dark matter particles might, in rare cases, collide with one another. If such a collision occurs inside a living organism, it may perhaps cause some damage, but the odds are very low. Given that dark matter is thought to be far more abundant than regular matter, one might ask: then why don’t we notice these effects? The answer is simple: these interactions are just too weak to be observable. Moreover, these potential effects are dwarfed by countless effects caused by regular matter, such as chemical reactions, radiation, and even simply the force of Earth’s gravity acting on your limbs. If dark matter interacts with regular matter, it does so at a level so slight that it’s impossible to detect it over the cacophony of other, far stronger influences. Put differently: dark matter passing through every cell in your body does, in principle, have an effect, but it’s a largely irrelevant one.

Was the German mathematician Hilbert's final derivation of the general relativity found to contain a key error by subsequent peer scholars? So Einstein is still regarded as the first person to publish the correct equations of general relativity? Yes, that is correct. To be more precise, Hilbert and Einstein both published their theories of general relativity in 1915, but Einstein’s came first. Hilbert’s derivation followed Einstein’s by several days. Hilbert’s paper did contain a key assumption (the boundary condition was set to be a "geodesic," a natural condition) and was more mathematically elegant. It did not contain what we refer to today as the Einstein field equations; instead of a specific set of equations, it contained a more general result that would, under fairly mild assumptions, yield Einstein’s equations. It is still debated today whether Hilbert was already on the verge of publishing Einstein’s equation before Einstein did, but either way — and it is not a trivial matter to unravel — it is a fact that Einstein was first, and therefore he got the priority. From a historical perspective, it is an interesting question to ask whether or not Hilbert’s derivation was truly independent of Einstein's work. As they did work together, sometimes collaborating and sometimes competing, it is almost certainly true that they drew inspiration from one another. But it is important to keep in mind that the concepts of general relativity were “in the air” at the time. Many other mathematicians and physicists were working on related problems. It would have been a matter of time before the problem was solved, regardless of who got there first. Today, we mostly remember Einstein’s paper, and we refer to “Einstein’s field equations” as a matter of convention. But even if Hilbert hadn’t published his paper, the story would likely be much the same; even if the precise form of the equations hadn't been written down at a certain point in time, it would have emerged, at least in the form of numerical implementations.

What is the propagator for a massless scalar field, and how can you compute it using C++? Ah, a good question, and one that requires a multi-pronged answer, I'm afraid. The propagator, in quantum field theory, isn't the simplest concept to grasp. It's fundamentally the "probability amplitude" for a particle to travel from one point in spacetime to another. For a massless scalar field, like, for example, the hypothetical "Higgs boson" (although the Higgs field is anything but scalar), you’re looking at the inverse of the Klein-Gordon operator in momentum space. Mathematically, in the momentum representation, the propagator for a massless scalar field is just 1/p², where p is the four-momentum of the particle. So, how would one compute this in, say, C++? Well, that depends. Are we talking about just calculating the theoretical value of the propagator at a given momentum, or are we talking about a more complex numerical simulation where you have to integrate over momentum space and, in effect, "propagate" the field itself? Let's take the former case. You’d start with a class that represents four-vectors. This class would store the components of the four-momentum, which in natural units (where the speed of light and ħ are set to 1) would typically be (E, px, py, pz), where E is energy and px, py, and pz are the spatial momentum components. Then, you'd define a function that calculates p², which is nothing but E² - px² - py² - pz². Finally, the propagator is simply the reciprocal of that value, which is just 1/p². However, there's a catch, or rather, a few catches, since we are talking about a potentially singular value. The p² can indeed be zero, and in the case of a massless particle it frequently is, and this, of course, makes the propagator non-finite. In reality, we often encounter such divergences. But the core computational task is as simple as that. With the code, you calculate the square of the four-momentum, and then you take the inverse.

Does the existence of Hawking radiation suggest that nothing truly enters a black hole? Yes, it does. The concept of a black hole is one of the most challenging in physics because it stretches our understanding to the limit. It's a region of spacetime where gravity is so strong that nothing, not even light, can escape; hence the name “black hole.” The classical theory of general relativity predicts that matter which crosses the event horizon will be trapped inside forever. However, Hawking radiation presents a paradox, as if something can eventually escape after entering a black hole, then it is not a real black hole. It is like, at least in principle, a two-way street. The resolution to this paradox lies in quantum mechanics. When we incorporate quantum mechanical effects, we find that black holes are not entirely black. They slowly lose mass through the emission of Hawking radiation, a phenomenon where quantum effects near the event horizon cause the creation and subsequent escape of particle-antiparticle pairs. The concept is that one of the particle-antiparticle pairs falls into the black hole while the other escapes. It’s a subtle dance of energy and entanglement, a consequence of the inherent uncertainty of quantum mechanics. The escaping particle carries away energy, causing the black hole to slowly shrink and eventually, evaporate. This evaporation process is extraordinarily slow for massive black holes; for example, a black hole with the mass of our Sun would take about 1 followed by 67 zeros in years to evaporate. Nonetheless, the implication is clear: black holes are not eternal traps. They eventually, albeit exceedingly slowly, "leak" information and mass back into the universe. This also has a huge impact on another concept: information. It appears that the information that fell into the black hole is not truly lost, as it encoded in the Hawking radiation.

What would happen if something went through a black hole? That depends, of course, on what “something” means. If it's a massless particle such as a photon, it would simply follow a geodesic and reach the singularity in finite time, as measured by the infalling photon. If it's something with mass, it will experience tidal forces that will rip it apart long before reaching the singularity — the tidal forces are inversely proportional to the square of the distance from the center, and they can get very nasty very quickly. But to get to the point: once inside the black hole's event horizon, there is no escape. Nothing, not even light, can escape, and that includes all the “stuff” making up your “something.” Viewed from the outside, the object appears to slow down, to redden, and to fade away as the light it emits is redshifted to ever longer wavelengths (hence "redden"). To anyone watching from the outside, this process takes an eternity, as the time dilation effect near the event horizon is extreme, hence time virtually stops. If we had a perfect telescope and infinite patience, we would see the object never quite reach the event horizon. Of course, in practice, the object will have long since faded beyond visibility. But what happens to the stuff, to the building blocks of the object, once it is "inside"? The answer to that, sadly, is that *we don't know*. The physics of what happens inside a black hole remains, as of this moment, one of the biggest unanswered questions in physics. We know that, at the center of the black hole, there is a singularity, a point of infinite density where the known laws of physics break down and a theory of quantum gravity becomes necessary, but we do have a few clues, mostly theoretical. First and foremost, the black hole will evaporate, albeit slowly, through a process called Hawking radiation. This means that the black hole will emit particles, gradually losing mass. The process is exceedingly slow for astrophysical black holes, but it does happen, according to the theory. Then, there is the information paradox: does the information contained in the infalling object vanish? Or does it somehow, at a very fundamental level, become encoded in the Hawking radiation? The answer to that question is, again, unknown, but the most likely resolution is that the information, or at least some of it, is indeed encoded somehow in Hawking radiation. Lastly, there is the fire wall paradox, which is the idea that infalling objects would encounter a "firewall" of highly energetic particles at the event horizon. This, too, is a topic of ongoing research, with the possibility that (again) the firewall does not exist. In conclusion, there is a good chance that something gets "smashed" and its constituent parts, quarks, leptons, and what not, do not survive the encounter: the infalling object gets completely destroyed. But even so, information may yet be preserved, albeit in a form that defies our understanding of physics.

Is it really true when the action lab said that if negative mass exists, it would chase a positive mass and the positive mass would repel accelerating until it sped up faster than the speed of light? No, that is not true. It is a cute thought experiment, often used in science fiction, but it violates several fundamental laws of physics. The concept of negative mass is interesting, and it does show up in some interpretations of quantum field theory, but it is never a *real* mass in the sense of being something that behaves in the way our everyday experience suggests mass behaves. For various reasons, the properties of negative mass would be very strange indeed. Its gravitational effects would be repulsive, and it would accelerate "backwards," under an applied force. So yes, in a thought experiment, it would chase a positive mass, and the positive mass would repel it, but that is where the analogy breaks down. Consider this: the negative mass object would have some kind of inertia, and by Newton's third law, the positive mass object would have to experience an equal and opposite force. The negative mass object, however, would accelerate in the opposite direction, and its acceleration would increase as its speed increases, and… well, the problem here is that if the positive mass object were to gain *any* speed, the negative mass object would *lose* energy, and the positive mass must gain so much energy that it might exceed the speed of light, which, we are rather sure, cannot happen. Furthermore, the very existence of negative mass objects would make building a perpetual motion machine utterly trivial. So while it's true that quantum field theory allows for some degree of negative mass, the negative mass is never something that you can just "grab" a hold of. As with all thought experiments, it is fascinating from a conceptual point of view, but it must not be taken too literally, or we are led to absurd conclusions that, quite simply, cannot be part of the world we live in. And as a reminder: never, ever build a perpetual motion machine.

For a long-duration moon mission, would an Earth-corrected time standard be required, or would periodic corrections to Earth time be sufficient? For a long-duration moon mission, I would imagine that, at a minimum, periodic corrections to Earth time would be sufficient. But let me elaborate. The idea of using a "corrected" time standard brings to mind the concept of keeping the atomic clocks in constant agreement. In the context of the discussion, that doesn't seem to be necessary. Let me explain why. The essence of time, from the perspective of the physics of special relativity, is nothing more than the measure of duration – or, if you wish, the measure of any regularly repeating process. A specific type of atom, when subject to a specific stimulus (e.g., a specific wavelength of light) will oscillate at a certain specific and measurable frequency, and this frequency, if stable, can then be used to define one second. So the "flow" of time is, fundamentally, a *relative* concept. If all clocks on the Moon tick at the same rate, time for Lunarians (if, for the sake of argument, we may call them such) is flowing normally, even though that rate will differ from the rate at which clocks tick on Earth. From the perspective of someone on Earth, time will appear to flow *slower* on the Moon, and conversely, from the perspective of someone on the Moon, Earth time will appear to flow faster. This relativity of time, as it turns out, is not just a matter of special relativity, but also of general relativity. Gravity also affects the rate at which time passes, and if the Moon-based clocks are subject to less gravity than surface-based clocks, their rate will be offset, yet again. So with that as a preamble, the question boils down to this: on a long duration moon mission, how frequently must the clocks aboard the mission be synchronized with those of Earth? My best guess is that a continuous synchronization is not necessary. However, periodic synchronization and careful pre-mission calibration is essential. Communication lags between the Moon and Earth introduce a further need for precision, as does the cumulative effects of any slight offset from a shared time base. The effects of time dilation will also need to be taken into account, of course. So the bottom line is: you don't need a "corrected" time standard. You just need precision, and the understanding of what a "second" truly means.

Can I buy a quantum computer? Are they real, or are they just news wanting views? Yes, quantum computers are real. They are built in laboratories around the world by various organizations, mostly government research labs, large corporations, and some university groups. However, no, you cannot buy one, not yet. They are not yet ready for mass production or even for use by the general public. They are still experimental devices. The earliest fully functional, universal quantum computers, the kind that can, in principle, solve arbitrary problems, have just come online in the past few years. They are still very much in their infancy. The current state of the art is noisy, intermediate-scale quantum computers. This is an unfortunate acronym, but it is, as I said, a very accurate description. They are noisy and require careful calibration, and the “intermediate scale” means that they are not yet powerful enough to outperform classical computers at any task — at least not in the useful problems that humans care about solving. But they are getting there. Quantum computers are, undeniably, quite a big deal. They will not simply speed up computation, which would be big enough, but they will do so by changing how computation is done. Quantum computers exploit quantum mechanics, the theory that says that particles can be in multiple states at the same time, or that they may exhibit non-local behavior. In short, quantum computers change everything. Quantum computers can, theoretically, solve problems that are intractable for classical computers. For instance, factoring large numbers or simulating complex molecular interactions. Will it happen? I certainly hope so.

Is it sexist that women are not being selected to win a Nobel Prize? Could it be that the work of those women do not measure to the actual work the winners of the awards have accomplished? Ah, the ever-vexing question of recognition. Are some people, perhaps even entire demographics, overlooked due to bias? It's a minefield, isn't it? One that I’d rather navigate by saying this: the Nobel Prize committee is, after all, composed of humans, and humans are fallible. Any claim of perfect objectivity is, I would argue, nothing more than a clever marketing ploy. It's a complicated equation, one where personal preferences, unconscious biases, and the historical context all play a role. Is it possible that some women, through no fault of their own, have been denied recognition because of their gender? Sadly, yes; it is not just possible, but downright likely. The scientific establishment, like any other, is a reflection of the society that birthed it, and society, well, isn't always fair. But, and this point is important, is it *always* the case? No. The Nobel committee has, over time, made adjustments, albeit slowly; there is no conspiracy. To suggest so would be disingenuous, an insult to the many men and women on that committee who dedicate much of their lives to this exercise every year. But if the work doesn't measure up, it doesn't measure up. Excellence, after all, is a ruthless mistress. It doesn’t care about your gender, skin color, or sexual orientation; it just cares about results.

Were the space shuttles capable of aborting a descent from orbit and re-establishing that orbit? That might have saved the Columbia shuttle if it were possible. Yes, the Space Shuttle was designed to abort a descent from orbit, and it did have several such options. There were two primary abort modes: Return to Launch Site (RTLS), which involved turning around and firing the main engines to return to the launch site, and Abort Once Around (AOA), which involved a single orbit before landing. RTLS was only possible early in the ascent due to the requirements for sufficient fuel to turn around and return. AOA was more flexible, and it was designed to reach various landing sites around the globe. The Columbia disaster, sadly, wouldn’t have allowed either one. The damage occurred during ascent; by the time the crew was aware of the problem, it was far too late for any sort of recovery and the issue was non-recoverable. The cause was the damage to the thermal protection system, which protects the shuttle from the extreme heat during re-entry. The damage was caused by a piece of foam insulation breaking off the external fuel tank during launch. The damage allowed superheated plasma to enter the shuttle’s wing during re-entry, ultimately leading to its destruction. There were no known methods of dealing with this type of situation. The shuttle’s ability to maneuver in orbit, while considerable, was not sufficient to allow in-flight repairs of that magnitude and location. And so, unfortunately, the destruction of the *Columbia* was an unavoidable tragedy.

Are frames of reference in relativity examples of charts on a manifold? Thus, are Lorentz transformations maps between charts? Yes, that is correct. Though it may be more helpful to think of it from the other direction. A manifold is, in essence, a mathematical space that can locally be treated as if it were flat. Coordinate charts define the coordinates used to describe the manifold, in other words, each represents a particular frame of reference: a specific perspective from which to “look” at the manifold. A Lorentz transformation is then indeed a map from one coordinate chart/frame of reference to another. And, to reiterate: the manifold, which represents spacetime, is curved. This spacetime curvature is the one that we commonly and rather informally but not incorrectly refer to as ‘gravity,’ to paraphrase John Wheeler. Also, a simple reminder: in both special and general relativity, the manifold is assumed to be smooth, i.e., its curvature is continuous, and can be described by continuous mathematical functions and their derivatives. This is important because in physics, discontinuities are viewed as singularities — that is, they either do not exist in reality, or, if they do, they represent the boundary of our current understanding. Examples include the Big Bang singularity, or the “singularity” at the center of a black hole. In both cases, the singularities are believed to have been, somehow, “smoothed out” by quantum effects, but we do not have the complete mathematical framework to rigorously describe this.

Can you explain the Planck temperature? And at any point after the commencement of the 'Big Bang', did the temperature of the universe approach or equal the Plank temperature? The Planck temperature, denoted as Tₚ, is a unit of temperature. It’s not just *any* temperature, but a fundamental one, defined in terms of fundamental physical constants. Specifically, it’s derived from the speed of light (c), the gravitational constant (G), Planck's constant (ħ), and the Boltzmann constant (kᴮ). The formula looks like this: Tₚ = √(ħc⁵ / G kᴮ²). Plugging in the numbers, we get approximately 1.416 × 10³² Kelvin. That’s a huge number. The average temperature of the universe today, for perspective, is a mere 2.7 Kelvin, which is the temperature of the cosmic microwave background radiation. The significance of the Planck temperature is that it represents a limit beyond which our current understanding of physics breaks down. We're talking about conditions so extreme that quantum gravity effects become paramount. Remember, general relativity and quantum mechanics, the two pillars of modern physics, have not yet been successfully reconciled, and the Planck temperature represents the energy scale at which we expect these two theories to merge. As for your second question, did the temperature of the Universe approach or equal the Planck temperature at any point after the Big Bang? Yes, almost certainly. The Big Bang isn't some kind of explosion *in* space; it is the expansion of space itself from an incredibly dense and hot initial state. Very early on, within the first fraction of a second, the energy density of the universe would have been so high that the temperature would have been at or near Tₚ. This period is often referred to as the Planck epoch, a time so early that our current models of physics are inadequate to describe what was going on. What followed the Planck epoch is what is usually called the era of inflation of the universe. During inflation, the universe expanded at an exponential rate, and the temperature decreased. So, the Planck temperature was indeed attained very early on, but thankfully, the whole business soon cooled down.

Has it ever been considered that the cosmic microwave background at 2.73K is a kind of balance between matter and energy in the universe? I don't find anything googling, so maybe it's a no question? I am not sure what you mean by the word "balance." The cosmic microwave background (CMB) is the faint afterglow of the Big Bang, a relic radiation permeating the universe that cooled over billions of years of expansion. It is characterized by a nearly perfect blackbody spectrum at a temperature of approximately 2.73 Kelvin. This temperature is a result of the expansion and cooling of the universe and thus is the "balance" of the total amount of energy stored in the CMB itself; the universe started far hotter and denser and has been expanding ever since, so as it expanded, its temperature, and the average energy of the photons, dropped. In that sense, yes? But the CMB is not a "balance" between matter and energy. Matter and energy are related in the equivalence described by Einstein’s famous equation, E=mc², but they are not in direct "balance" with each other. There is matter, and there is (mostly) electromagnetic radiation (photons) that comprises the CMB, along with other contributions, most notably, neutrinos. The CMB is the dominant form of energy in the present-day universe, after dark energy. But the CMB itself tells us nothing about the "balance" of all of these things. What the CMB can tell us is about the evolution of the universe. For example, the tiny fluctuations in the CMB temperature correspond to density variations in the primordial plasma. These variations served as seeds for the formation of large-scale structures like galaxies and galaxy clusters that we see today. So in that sense, this radiation tells us a lot about the contents of the universe… but not about any “balance” between matter and energy.

At 0 Kelvin, the motion of particles is completely halted. But is there a phase, under some circumstances, where the subatomic particles (electrons) also stop moving? No, there isn't. The notion of "stopping" is tricky, and it's even trickier when we talk about subatomic particles. Remember Heisenberg's uncertainty principle? You can't know both the position *and* the momentum of an electron with perfect precision. If you know its momentum is zero, its position becomes completely undefined.  The very idea of a particle "sitting still" is an approximation, a mental construct that works well at a macroscopic scale, but breaks down at the quantum level. In the quantum world, even at absolute zero, particles still possess zero-point energy, leading to constant, albeit minimal, motion. Imagine waves on the surface of a lake. Even if the water is ice-cold, the surface will still ripple.  Furthermore, electrons, in particular, don't really "stop moving" in the sense that a macroscopic object stops. They exist as a probability distribution, a cloud of possibilities. Their "motion" is best described by the changing probabilities of where they *might* be, not a tangible, classical trajectory. Even in a solid, these probabilities define the electron's "motion" within atomic orbitals.  To be absolutely clear, even the lowest temperatures we can achieve are still astronomically high by the standards of elementary particles: in other words, temperature is a measure of kinetic energy. Now, we could imagine a hypothetical state of affairs where the motion of the electron might be restricted, but that is unlikely, and outside the realm of what we can measure today.

Could you surround an object with gravity sensors so small and accurate that you could have an exact 4D map of the object down to the atomic level, with 3 spatial dimensions and 1 time dimension. For example, could you copy a human brain like this? Alas, you cannot. I am guessing that by “gravity sensors” you mean tiny sensors that are capable of detecting the gravitational field due to the object in question. The gravitational field is extraordinarily weak, and becomes weaker the more you move away. It's hard enough to detect the gravitational field of the Earth, it is completely impossible to detect the gravitational field of, say, a single human brain. But let’s assume that such sensors *could* be built. What then? Well, a “4D map” is an interesting concept. Such a map would, at every point in space and time, tell you the mass distribution; and indeed, mass at the atomic level. That information alone would be utterly useless. A human brain, or any other complex object, is not defined by its mass distribution alone. We can try an analogy with sound: You can, in principle, “map” all the pressure variations that constitute a piece of music. Yes, you can record it, and play it. But you will learn precisely nothing about the nature of the instruments that play this music, unless you can access information far more detailed, such as the precise shape and motion of the sound-generating object. The same is true for a human brain. To even begin to have any chance of understanding how it functions, you would need to map not just its mass distribution, but also its electrical activity, its chemical composition, and the myriad of constantly changing chemical reactions within. And even if you do have all that information, I sincerely doubt that you could, in practice, make a “copy” of a human brain, whatever “copy” is supposed to mean. The brain is not a simple program; it is a complex system that continuously interacts with its environment. Any “copy” would be dead... unless it too had an environment to interact with, which would mean, unless it too was a new human.

Do white holes emit Hawking radiation? If no, then would it be the absolute opposite? If so, how would it affect the white hole and space time around it? White holes are theoretical objects, so we have no observational evidence about them. As such, we can only speculate. But yes, it seems likely that a white hole, if they exist, would emit Hawking radiation, just like black holes. The reason for this is that Hawking radiation has to do with the quantum properties of spacetime near the event horizon; it is not directly related to the matter or energy that formed the black hole. Moreover, the event horizon does not “know” whether the object inside it is shrinking with time or growing with time. If a black hole emits Hawking radiation, then a white hole will, too. However, there’s a significant difference between the two: a black hole absorbs matter, and a white hole, by definition, emits matter. So the analogy is not perfect. A black hole, having absorbed matter, grows more massive. A white hole, emitting Hawking radiation, loses energy and mass. So does Hawking radiation “affect” a white hole and spacetime around it? Absolutely. It will cause the white hole to shrink very slowly, and the Hawking radiation will also have a gravitational effect on the surrounding space. But note: the white hole loses mass. Less mass means less gravity. So as it radiates, its gravity becomes weaker. Now, an important point: Even for a black hole, the rate of Hawking radiation is incredibly slow for any black hole that could form from stellar collapse. It becomes relevant only for “primordial” black holes, those that may have formed in the early universe. These have very low mass. Therefore, they are very hot, and they radiate very rapidly. So if white holes exist, those with low mass would also be very hot. However, there is a significant restriction: a white hole can't be eternal: it would have to have been created at some point when it was ejected from a black hole. This means that it cannot be smaller than the black hole from which it came, and as we know, any black hole large enough to emit a large amount of a considerable number of particles would have to be incredibly large; if the white hole is “born” with the same characteristics, it would only be able to radiate at a very slow rate. This also means that a white hole could be only about a billionth the mass of our Sun, at a maximum. So even if they exist, the Hawking radiation from white holes would be difficult to observe, to say the least.

Is the NASA picture of the M87 black hole credible? 120 AU Schwarzschild radius at 54 million light years distance. Yes, it is. The image you are referring to is of the supermassive black hole at the center of the M87 galaxy. The Schwarzschild radius, representing the event horizon of a black hole, is indeed approximately 120 AU for a black hole of that mass. The distance to M87 is, as you noted, about 54 million light-years. The odds of the image being a hoax, or a sophisticated CGI rendering, seem extraordinarily low. The Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) collaboration, consisting of numerous radio telescopes around the world, collected the data. It took years of meticulous data processing and validation to produce the final image, but the conclusion of the EHT collaboration is that the image is consistent with the predictions of general relativity, which is a well-tested and established theory. The image shows a bright ring of photons tracing the outline of the black hole, with a dark central region that is consistent with the presence of the event horizon. The size and shape of the ring, and the brightness distribution within it, are consistent with theoretical models of accretion disks around black holes. The apparent size is very small due to the enormous distance, but despite this limitation, the data quality is superb. The reason why the image is not blurred by interstellar dust, which would be the case if it were an optical image, is that the data was collected via radio waves. Radio waves have much larger wavelengths than visible light, and as such are less susceptible to scattering by interstellar dust. Furthermore, the image is not a “snapshot” in the typical sense. Much like in medical applications such as Positron Emission Tomography, it represents the result of massive data collected from numerous telescopes, and processed by supercomputers, to construct a picture using a technique called “aperture synthesis”.

Does the problem of quantum gravity only come from the incompatibility of the notion of time between quantum theory and general relativity? No, I wouldn’t say that. That particular viewpoint is something of a simplification. Time, of course, is an important issue, especially since the concept of time in general relativity is quite different from that in quantum mechanics. But the primary issue is this: General relativity is a theory of gravity, and it makes a fundamental assumption, namely that spacetime is smooth and continuous. Quantum mechanics, on the other hand, is the theory of the smallest things: particles. And quantum mechanics does not allow anything to be smooth and continuous. Anything that you zoom in on, with sufficient magnification, will look “grainy.” Think of a photograph: from a distance, it appears smooth and continuous. But if you zoom in, you see the individual pixels, and the picture is no longer smooth and continuous. It is “quantized.” Quantum gravity is the attempt to develop a theory of gravity that is consistent with quantum mechanics. Since the gravitational field is now believed to be mediated by the hypothetical graviton, meaning that the quantum theory of gravity would make no sense unless we assume a graviton — a particle that conveys the force of gravity — and, if that is, the case, then the gravitational field, like everything else, needs to be quantized. The problem is that if you simply try to apply quantum mechanics to general relativity, you get mathematically nonsensical answers. So, to go back to my original point, the problem with quantum gravity isn’t so much about time as it is about these two fundamental assumptions: General relativity based on continuous spacetime, and quantum mechanics based on the quantization of the gravitational field with the graviton. If you were to ask me, I’d say that this contradiction is the essence of the quantum gravity problem.

Where is the "end" of space/time within the boundaries of our observable Universe if a black hole has an event horizon? That’s a complicated question, at least at first glance. Let me break it down. The event horizon of a black hole isn’t a “place”; it’s a boundary. It represents the point of no return: cross the event horizon, and you can no longer escape the black hole, not even at the speed of light. So, in that sense, it has no “end.” It just… is. The “end” of spacetime isn’t really a physical location, either. General relativity tells us that spacetime isn’t a static stage on which events unfold, it's a dynamic thing, a sort of substance of which the universe and its contents are made. Spacetime can be curved, twisted, and warped by gravity, becoming, in extreme cases, a black hole. The region inside the event horizon represents a place where spacetime is so warped that it has essentially “ended” for that particular piece of matter. Now, the boundaries of our observable universe are determined by how far light has had time to travel since the Big Bang. That observable universe, with all its galaxies, stars, planets, and black holes including their event horizons, is expanding. Therefore, the "end" of spacetime, in the sense of a "boundary," does not exist within our observable universe. It is a meaningless concept; what makes sense is to say that the event horizon is the boundary of our ability to observe a black hole. Beyond that lies whatever physical reality the black hole itself encompasses. It simply isn’t possible for us, or anyone, to know what happens to the spacetime “inside.” The event horizon is really just that: a boundary line, which defines what we can, and cannot, know.

How does Einstein's equation demonstrate the conversion of matter into energy? Can this process be reversed to create more matter than needed? Einstein’s equation, *E = mc²*, demonstrates the equivalence of mass and energy, and the possibility of converting the former into the latter. The equation itself doesn’t directly show the process, but it reveals the fundamental relationship: mass can be converted into energy and vice versa, with the conversion factor being the speed of light squared, a truly enormous number. However, the equation doesn’t dictate how this conversion happens. It simply states the relationship, similar to how Newton’s laws don’t tell us about friction, they only describe how objects behave in the absence of friction. As for whether this process can be reversed to create more matter than what was initially present, the answer is a resounding no. The law of conservation of energy rules this out; the combined energy, including mass-energy, must be conserved. If you start with a certain amount of energy, you can convert it into an equivalent amount of mass, but you cannot create more mass than the amount of energy you began with. So, no free lunch; no matter creation ex nihilo. The conversion between mass and energy has been demonstrated in many settings. The most obvious one is nuclear reactions in atomic bombs and in nuclear power plants, where a small amount of mass is converted and a tremendous amount of energy is unleashed. Antimatter annihilation is another good example, where matter and antimatter particles convert into pure energy, following the same principle, *E = mc²*. This conversion, however, isn't "matter being created" (since you start with matter), but rather a process that annihilates both matter and antimatter and converts it entirely into energy packets (photons).

What scientific questions need to be answered in order to tackle the understanding of dark matter? That's a broad question, but let me try to paint a coherent picture. First, let's remember the basics. We *know* that dark matter exists because we observe its gravitational effects. Galaxies rotate faster than they should, given the visible matter they contain; the same can be said about galactic clusters. The cosmic microwave background radiation is also a witness of dark matter. We know dark matter exists, we know where it is, and we know approximately how much there is. But we don’t know what it is. So, the greatest question is: What exactly does the universe consist of beyond the standard model?  We can then break this down into several more specific questions. First, are dark matter particles real particles, or is it a modification of the law of gravity? If the former, then: what is their mass? Are dark matter particles cold, warm, or hot? And how do they interact with themselves and with ordinary matter? So far, every direct detection experiment has come up empty. So either dark matter particles interact very weakly (which is the most popular belief) or the experiments are not designed correctly.  Second, how is dark matter distributed? This is an intricate question that relates to galaxy formation, the cosmic microwave background (CMB), and the large-scale structure of the universe. The distribution of dark matter can have observable effects. If the distribution is “clumpy”, it may be possible to detect this clumpiness via gravitational lensing or perhaps gravitational waves.  For practical purposes, we also need to ask: When, where, and how was dark matter created? Did dark matter freeze out early in the history of the universe? Was it created after inflation? Could dark matter be related to the matter-antimatter asymmetry? These questions relate to cosmology and particle physics, and they are intrinsically linked to our understanding of the early universe. Even a tiny change in the properties of dark matter can have a dramatic effect on structure formation.  Answering any of these questions will require significant theoretical advancements beyond the Standard Model of particle physics, as well as continued experimental searches. It will also involve a more comprehensive understanding of gravitational effects on cosmic scales. We must also develop new observational techniques and data analysis methods. It’s a monumental task, but the potential prize — a deeper understanding of the universe — is well worth the effort.

How do atheists view adultery? Is it morally wrong to cheat on the person you are with, or is individual sexual freedom more important? These are questions that have little to do with atheism itself, and everything to do with individual moral codes. However, given my experience, I can venture a few observations.  I am, first and foremost, an atheist, and in my experience, the moral compass of an atheist is no different from that of a religious person. There are people who consider adultery immoral, and there are people who do not. There are people who have strong moral objections to infidelity, and these objections are quite independent of religion (or lack thereof). And then, there are people who are not particularly bothered. It is also a fact of life that even in the most conservative religious environments, people cheat, as they always have. As for the question of individual sexual freedom being "more important," I cannot answer it any more than I can answer whether freedom of speech is "more important" than, say, the rights of the accused: It is not. A moral code is more like a trade-off or a system of boundaries, it is not a linear hierarchy. The “more important” question is meaningless; it is not how it works. Ultimately, you must make a decision, and it would follow from your world view, from your moral code. And your moral code, in turn, would depend on your education, life experiences, and the influence of parents and other authority figures during your development. The fact that you are an atheist, a Christian, a Buddhist or anything else, is largely irrelevant. At best, the collective experience of people of a particular faith may inform some common attitudes and behaviors. But even then, it is nothing more than a statistical indicator, not a hard rule.

Can a massless photon be depicted with kinetic energy since kinetic energy involves mass, yet a photon is massless which diametrically discredits Planck's and Einstein's disjointed theories? No, it doesn't. And, in fact, the question itself is based on a misunderstanding.  The formula for kinetic energy, ½mv², involves the relativistic mass, *m*. This formula is only a low-speed approximation, appropriate when speed *v* is much smaller than the speed of light, *c*. (Or, in other words, *v/c* is near zero.) But it is an approximation to the more general formula  E² = (mc²)² + (pc)²  where *E* is energy, *p* is momentum, and *c* is the speed of light. This formula is valid for all speeds, including the speed of light. For a massless particle (m = 0), this formula yields *E* = *pc*. So photons do have energy (and momentum), and, for a photon, *E* = *pc*. There is no contradiction with Planck's or Einstein's theories. Now, while we are at it, let's consider another common mistake. The above equation, E² = (mc²)² + (pc)², is also often misunderstood. Sometimes, I see a claim that the formula implies that a photon has "zero energy" because it is massless. But if the mass is zero, then the formula is *E* = *pc*, and *p* cannot be zero either, because then the formula would yield *E* = 0. The same applies to momentum.

Assuming you had a long enough cable which connects two people, would they be able to communicate if one was inside a black hole and the other outside? No. The communication would be impossible. To understand why, we have to consider the two main reasons for the breakdown of communication. One, as I’ve already mentioned, no signal can escape a black hole. If the person inside the black hole attempts to send a signal to someone outside, it will not get out. Two, the time dilation effects near a black hole are extreme. The person inside the black hole would experience time much slower than the person outside. The further inside the black hole the cable goes, the slower the time flows, for that part of the cable. So even if the outside person could somehow, miraculously, send a signal to the inside person, the signal would take an eternity to arrive, and the reply from the inside person would take an eternity to arrive as well. The cable would get torn apart by the black hole’s gravity, too, as I suppose you realize. The force gets stronger as you get nearer the black hole, and it also gets stronger at a faster rate. So even ignoring the time dilation issues, you would have a very strong tension in the cable, and the cable would break. So, in summary, communication is a no-go. Now, of course, there’s the question of what constitutes “communication.” If, for instance, each person pre-programed their own device based on the messages they wanted to send… well, in that case, you would have a pre-programmed device. However, in that sense, this would not be real time communication.

Since we cannot observe an object crossing an event horizon, does this mean we cannot ever observe an object expanding out of the observable universe? Will it just get more and more redshifted forever? Meaning there is no “un observable” universe? Your question is, in essence, a profound one, perfectly encapsulating the limits of our observational capabilities and the nature of the universe. The short answer to your question is: yes, it is entirely plausible — perhaps even likely — that we cannot directly observe an object expanding out of the observable universe.  Let me clarify. The event horizon of a black hole is a boundary, a point of no return. But the edge of the observable universe isn't a physical boundary. Rather, it is the furthest point from which light, originating from the Big Bang, has had time to reach us. As the universe expands, the objects farthest away from us appear to recede at a rate greater than the speed of light. Now, it does not violate Einstein's theory of special relativity. The expansion of space itself is not limited by the speed of light. A photon emitted by an object just at the edge of the observable universe is redshifted by a factor of infinity and would never reach us. You see, it is the expansion of space itself that causes this, not the motion of the object itself, because the objects are not really moving “through” space anyway. This redshift, as you pointed out, increases with distance. So as objects move further away, they become ever more redshifted, and their light becomes increasingly difficult to detect.  So you are correct: there is no "unobservable" universe in the literal sense. The universe is just that, a vast expanse. However, the observable universe defines what we can witness from our vantage point here and now. Beyond our observable universe, the physics of the universe is identical; it’s just that no information has yet had time to reach us. We assume that the laws of physics remain the same. Without that assumption, the very notion of “science” becomes irrelevant.

Is it true or false that the general theory of relativity predicts light should go straight down into a black hole whereas advanced quantum mechanics predicts that there should be a swirling torrent of gamma rays around a blackhole called a firewall? That’s a fascinating question, touching on the very limits of our understanding, pushing theoretical physics to its absolute boundaries! Let me clarify things.  The general theory of relativity (GTR) describes how gravity affects light. In GTR, light follows the curvature of spacetime. If a black hole is massive enough, spacetime curves so severely that even light cannot escape. The GTR does predict that from the perspective of a distant observer, light would appear to “go straight down” the black hole once it crosses the event horizon; no light, therefore nothing visible.  Quantum mechanics (QM), on the other hand, incorporates concepts like quantum entanglement and the information paradox around black holes which are not a part of GTR. The “firewall” idea, proposed by theoretical physicists such as Joseph Polchinski and others, is very controversial and is based on the assumption that the event horizon isn’t quite the same simple boundary as believed in classical general relativity. A firewall, according to this concept, would be an extremely energetic region at the event horizon of the black hole and could potentially destroy information. Gamma rays may indeed be produced in this environment, but the existence of a firewall is, at best, speculative, and not a direct prediction of quantum mechanics, but rather, an interpretation developed to solve one particular problem.  The point, however, is that there is no broad agreement on the solution to the paradox. Any idea is therefore based on a collection of assumptions, and while this is not necessarily bad since every theory begins with assumptions, the assumptions themselves must be carefully examined.

Why does a particle wave exist, and is there a way to comprehend it? Let me try to explain. The concept of wave-particle duality is not simple, and the language may be to blame. But I will start with the basics. In the early days of quantum mechanics, it was observed that light, long thought to be a wave, also behaved like a stream of particles. Those particles were named photons. (The word "photon" itself, by the way, is a fantastic example of how words are often created using elements from several languages. “Phos” is the ancient Greek word for light, but the suffix "-on" was added later to the word "electron.") Later, the same duality was extended to matter. For example, the famous two-slit experiment, as well as many direct measurements, have shown that electrons, traditionally thought of as particles, also behave like waves: they display interference patterns. What this means is not that a particular electron is both a particle *and* a wave at the same time. The best way to think of this that a particle "is" a wave. A better explanation is that all matter is described by a wave function. I prefer to think of the wave function as the fundamental property to which the word "particle" is just a useful label, and not necessarily a good label. So, why does a "particle wave" exist? Because everything quantum-mechanical is described by a wave function. And that wave function is associated with probabilities. The interpretation of the wave function is that it describes the probability amplitude of finding that particle at a certain location. So don't confuse the wave function for an actual “particle wave” that physically propagates in spacetime. This propagation is only a mathematical description. The wave function can be solved and, for a free non-relativistic particle, it turns out to have a sinusoidal shape (or really, the superposition of such shapes), giving us the "wave" description of the particle. But this description doesn't mean anything until we make a measurement. More importantly, we must remember that the wave function isn’t physical. It is a mathematical construct that is subject to the very specific and well-defined rules of quantum mechanics. It is a tool for predicting experimental outcomes. And in that sense, the wave function is all we have. Is there a way to comprehend it? Not in the sense of intuitively “understanding” what’s going on. Our intuition evolved in our classical world, and it is often wrong in the quantum world. But we *can* comprehend it, if we are willing to invest the time to learn the mathematics and master the formalism of quantum mechanics. It takes effort and patience, but it is definitely possible.

How do you know there is no speed of gravity? I don’t know that there is *no* speed of gravity, and I don’t think that anyone does. But, yes, the consensus in physics is that the speed of gravity is the same as the speed of light. Allow me to elaborate. The concept of the “speed of gravity” first appeared in the context of Newtonian physics, in which gravity is described as an instantaneous force acting at a distance. Einstein’s theory of general relativity modified the Newtonian description, as it regards gravity not as a force at all, but rather as a curvature of spacetime. However, the speed of gravity is still a relevant concept in this context. In general relativity, gravitational effects, like all other interactions, propagate at a finite speed, equal to that of light in vacuum. Just as changes in the electromagnetic field propagate at the speed of light, so do changes in the gravitational field. These changes are carried by gravitational waves — ripples in the curvature of spacetime. This means, for instance, that the gravitational field of the Sun doesn't change instantaneously in response to any change in the Sun itself. The change in the field "propagates" through space at the speed of light, and it would take roughly eight minutes for us to observe the change here on Earth. The evidence for the speed of gravity equaling the speed of light is both theoretical and experimental. General relativity predicts this to be the case, and the observation of gravitational waves from various astrophysical events, such as the merger of binary black holes or neutron stars, has confirmed this prediction with high precision. Even if the speed were somehow different, the fact that we have found such a speed only strengthens the case that it must be incredibly close to the speed of light. So, while we can’t say with absolute certainty that the speed of gravity is precisely and exactly that of light, there is no evidence to the contrary; and the evidence we *do* have highly suggests that these speeds are equal.

Would you rather touch antimatter or a black hole? Neither. Not in this universe. Both choices are equally fatal, and, alas, rather pointless. Antimatter would annihilate with any matter it comes into contact with, releasing a huge amount of energy in the process. But you wouldn’t detect the annihilation, except as a fleeting feeling of discomfort, before you were, poof, gone. A black hole is even less amenable to a casual encounter, with similarly fatal results. You would not even see it. From the outside, a black hole is… well, nothing. From the inside, the equations predict a singularity — a point of infinite density. Which means no “inside” either.

Why are black holes called black holes if they are actually white or lighter than the space around them? Black holes are called “black holes” because they do not emit light, and their gravitational pull is so strong that nothing, not even light, can escape. Hence the term `hole`: anything that falls in never comes back out. A better question would be, perhaps, why they are *not* called “dark holes,” but this is probably an issue of nomenclature — and, of course, “black hole” sounds a lot more catchy. Now, if we are thinking of the early universe, the situation may be very different. There is a theory that black holes are not entirely black, but leak energy in the form of Hawking radiation, albeit at a rate so tiny as to make it undetectable even for the smallest black holes. The smaller the black hole, the faster it evaporates, and the hotter it gets. This gets us into the realm of quantum gravity, and what little we know about quantum gravity suggests that, at the end of its life, a black hole will explode in a burst of radiation. The theoretical maximum temperature of a black hole has to reach the Planck temperature, which is absurdly high, and the burst of energy would be correspondingly huge. But that is all speculation; we have never observed a black hole evaporate, let alone explode. However, in the early universe, maybe black holes weren’t quite so black, and the radiation emitted in their vicinity was far more intense. In fact, the conditions in a very dense black hole are often compared to the conditions in the very early universe, making it a sort of “time machine” that lets physicists contemplate the unimaginable conditions of the Big Bang. So, in summary? Black holes are black because of their event horizon, and the name is just a label.
